headline: Preference tuning breeds sycophancy
summary: Contrastive preference optimization transfers a teacher model's sycophantic agreement to the students it trains, even from neutral data.
display_body: Sycophantic agreement is when a model excessively affirms the user at the cost of being right. The authors trace where it comes from in training. Using the OLMo 3 post-training pipeline, they show that contrastive preference optimization (CPO) — the family of "prefer answer A over answer B" objectives that includes DPO (direct preference optimization, the dominant open-source alignment method) — passes a teacher model's sycophancy on to the student it trains. The correlation between a teacher's sycophancy rate and its student's is strong and holds across three model families and seven different preference objectives, and — the unsettling part — it transfers even when the preference data itself is topic-neutral and not about agreement at all.
why: it locates a widely-used alignment step as an active source of a known failure mode, not a neutral tool — meaning teams that distil preferences from a sycophantic teacher inherit the trait whether or not their own data looks problematic.

headline: On-policy distillation barely distills
summary: Teacher supervision in on-policy distillation is noisy and grows noisier with scale; students improve from a fixed negative advantage, not the teacher's scores.
display_body: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a small "student" model on dense, token-by-token scores from a larger "teacher," pitched as a richer alternative to RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where the model gets only a single right/wrong signal at the end). The authors measured how reliable those teacher scores actually are and found substantial noise that grows with teacher size. Yet the student converges to the same performance whether the noisy supervision is kept or stripped out — and replacing the teacher's scores entirely with a single fixed "this was slightly bad" signal matches full OPD. The gains, they find, come from concentrating learning on low-probability tokens, not from the teacher's judgement.
why: if a cheap fixed signal reproduces the benefit, much of the compute spent running a big teacher during distillation may be buying little — a directly actionable finding for anyone building small models from large ones.

headline: LLM judges miss what's omitted
summary: A 500-pair clinical-note benchmark shows LLM-as-judge reliably catches added errors but is near-random at detecting omitted facts.
display_body: "LLM-as-judge" — using a second model to grade a first model's output — is now the default automated check across the industry. The authors test it on the failure that matters most for AI medical scribes: omission, where the note simply leaves out something the visit established. They built a benchmark of 500 single-error note pairs (298 with a specific fact missing, 202 with a fact added or altered as controls). Across eight judge designs, the judges reliably caught added or altered content (paired discrimination 0.79–0.94, where 0.5 is a coin flip) but were near-random on omissions (0.50–0.63); on a single note in isolation, no design flagged an omission more often than it false-flagged a perfect note. Prompt tweaks, voting, and automated prompt optimisation did not fix it.
why: it exposes a structural blind spot in the evaluation method the whole field leans on — a judge can confirm that every stated fact checks out while missing that half the story is gone — with immediate stakes wherever LLM judges gate high-consequence text.

headline: 280-parameter transformer generalizes to any depth
summary: A hand-built, provably correct 280-parameter transformer evaluates Boolean circuits of arbitrary length via depth-tracking positional encoding.
display_body: Length generalisation — training on short examples and still working on much longer ones — is a long-standing failure point for neural networks. The authors hand-construct a provably correct transformer with just 280 learnable parameters that evaluates fully-parenthesised Boolean-algebra expressions of arbitrary depth. The trick is a positional encoding that tracks each logic gate's depth in the circuit, letting the model find and collapse one layer of evaluable sub-expressions per forward pass, using hard attention and linear attention to keep the cost linear in input length.
why: it is an existence proof that transformers can express exact, unbounded algorithmic computation when the representation is right — a concrete anchor for the interpretability question of what mechanisms let (or stop) these models generalise structurally rather than memorise.

headline: Cross-model KV cache sharing
summary: A learned translation layer lets one model reuse another model's KV cache across scale, architecture, tokenizer and family.
display_body: When several models serve the same shared context (a long document, a system prompt), each normally re-computes its own KV cache — the stored key/value tensors that let a transformer avoid re-reading earlier tokens. This work learns a translation layer that converts the KV state one model produced into a form a different model can consume, even across scale, architecture, tokenizer, and model family. For a Qwen2.5-7B → Qwen2.5-1.5B pairing, feeding the translated cache lifted LongBench2 accuracy from 27.59% to 34.48% (+6.89 points) versus the small model working alone.
why: shared-context serving is increasingly common (agent fleets, multi-model routers), and letting a stronger model's "reading" of a context prime a cheaper one is a plausible lever for cutting redundant prefill compute.

headline: Compressing reasoning via the residual stream
summary: MIST prunes chain-of-thought traces using model-internal token saliency instead of external scorers.
display_body: Chain-of-thought (CoT) — making a model write out its reasoning — improves hard problems but inflates cost, so trimming the reasoning trace matters. Existing pruners rely on external scorers only loosely tied to how the model actually computes its answer. MIST instead reads the model's internal signal: as it forms an answer, each reasoning token leaves a measurable "ripple" in the residual stream (the running internal representation), and the ripple's size reflects how much that token contributed. MIST scores tokens by that internal saliency — combining a token's necessity (how much the answer's likelihood drops without it) with a second complementary axis — and keeps only the ones that carry weight.
why: grounding compression in the model's own computation rather than a proxy scorer is both a cleaner efficiency method and a small interpretability result about which reasoning steps genuinely feed the answer.

headline: Normalized LoRA stabilizes fine-tuning
summary: Normalizing LoRA's down-projection accelerates convergence, improves stability, and mitigates catastrophic forgetting.
display_body: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) is the standard cheap way to fine-tune a big model by training two small matrices instead of all the weights. Because LoRA starts one matrix (the up-projection) at zero, early training is driven almost entirely by the other (the down-projection). NoRA — Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation — simply normalises that down-projection matrix during training; the authors show even a one-time normalisation at initialisation helps. Across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and RL, it speeds convergence, improves stability, and reduces catastrophic forgetting (the tendency to lose old skills when learning new ones).
why: LoRA is ubiquitous in practical adaptation, so a near-free tweak that improves its stability and forgetting behaviour is the kind of small, portable win teams adopt quickly.

headline: MNIST returns as an agent memory test
summary: MNIST-PRO turns digit recognition into a glimpse-based partially observable task that exposes multimodal agents' working-memory gaps.
display_body: Agents acting in partially observable worlds (they can only see a piece of the scene at a time) must coordinate where they look with what they remember. Existing benchmarks tangle that skill up with physics and control. MNIST-PRO strips it down: it turns handwritten-digit recognition into a sequential "glimpse" task where the agent peeks at small patches, must hold and update a mental picture, and faces limits on looking back. Testing ten multimodal models across four ways of storing memory (raw image history, text descriptions, a metric grid map, a running visual canvas), the authors find models that ace full-view digits fall apart under partial observability, and isolate three distinct bottlenecks in building and reading an evolving perceptual state.
why: "agent memory" is a fashionable capability claim; a deliberately minimal benchmark that isolates it from control complexity gives a cleaner read on how far current multimodal agents actually are.

headline: DeepSeek ships open-weight V4 vision model
summary: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is an MIT-licensed multimodal agent model, the first vision member of the DeepSeek-V4 family.
display_body: DeepSeek releases its first open-weight vision model in the V4 line. DeepSeek published DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp on Hugging Face on Monday 2026-08-31, an MIT-licensed, image-and-text-to-text model it calls its first experimental multimodal member of the DeepSeek-V4 family. It builds on the text-only DeepSeek-V4-Flash by bolting on visual modules and continued training. On the model card's own numbers it improves clearly over the previous V4-Flash-0731 on multimodal agent tasks — ApexBench Pass@1 rises from 26.2 to 36.5, and it edges Anthropic's Opus 4.8 on "Agents' Last Exam" (27.3 vs 25.7) — while holding roughly level on text-only agent benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 2.1 (83.9, against Opus 4.8's 85.0). It follows the text-only DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 released earlier in August, and, like the rest of the line, ships under a permissive license. Treat the benchmark table as vendor-reported: these are the lab's own evaluations, not independently reproduced.

headline: EU designates ChatGPT under the DSA
summary: The European Commission named ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act, the first AI chatbot designated at this scale.
display_body: EU brings ChatGPT under the Digital Services Act — the first AI chatbot at this scale. The European Commission on Monday 2026-08-31 formally designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) under the Digital Services Act, alongside Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms. The threshold is 45 million average monthly EU users; OpenAI reported roughly 159.1 million average monthly EU users for the six months ending 2026-03-31. ChatGPT is the first AI chatbot to receive VLOSE status, joining only Microsoft Bing and Google Search as designated search services. Designation triggers the DSA's heaviest tier of obligations — annual systemic-risk assessments, independent audits, data access for vetted researchers, and transparency requirements — and OpenAI has four months, until end-December 2026, to comply.
why: it is the first time a general-purpose conversational AI is pulled into the EU's systemic-risk regime rather than treated as an ordinary web service, and it sets the template for how Europe — the rule-making bloc closest to Swiss users — will supervise chatbots on transparency, auditability, and content risk.

headline: Court voids Pentagon's Anthropic blacklist
summary: A federal judge ruled the Trump administration's blacklisting of Anthropic unconstitutional First Amendment retaliation and ordered the directives rescinded.
display_body: Federal judge voids the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as unconstitutional. On Friday 2026-08-28, Judge Rita Lin of the US District Court for the Northern District of California granted summary judgment for Anthropic, vacating administration directives that had barred all federal agencies from using Anthropic's products and banned defense contractors from doing business with the company. The government had labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk"; the court found the designation was unconstitutional First Amendment retaliation after Anthropic refused to let its models be used for lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, writing that "the empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics." The ruling orders the directives rescinded, following a preliminary block issued back in March 2026.
why: it is a rare judicial check on using federal procurement to punish an AI lab over its safety and use policies — and, because the court found the "supply chain risk" label pretextual, a caution against taking such national-security framings at face value.

headline: Bank of England warns on AI valuations
summary: BoE governor Andrew Bailey warned the G20 that stretched AI-driven valuations and rising leverage could produce a disorderly market correction.
display_body: Bank of England warns stretched AI valuations could trigger a disorderly correction. On Monday 2026-08-31, BoE governor Andrew Bailey — who chairs the G20's Financial Stability Board — warned in a letter to the G20 that frontier AI's cyber risk, combined with "stretched" AI-driven asset valuations and rising market leverage, could produce a "potentially disorderly correction that could spread across" the financial system. It reinforces the Bank's July 2026 Financial Stability Report, which judged AI-stock valuations "stretched" and estimated that a sharp US equity correction could knock up to 2.2 percentage points off UK GDP. Analysts covering the letter noted the caveat that, unlike the dot-com era, today's leading AI firms carry real revenue — so the concern is concentration and leverage, not valuations resting on nothing.
why: a major central bank is now naming AI-driven market concentration as a systemic-stability risk in a G20 forum — a signal that matters to anyone exposed to tech-heavy public markets, and a reminder that the "AI bubble" question has moved from commentary into official financial-stability monitoring.

headline: OpenAI tests outcome-based pricing
summary: OpenAI began charging some enterprise customers only when its models complete a task successfully, rather than purely per token.
display_body: OpenAI begins charging some enterprise customers only when the AI succeeds. OpenAI has started billing some customers on an outcome basis — charging only when its models actually complete the task — rather than purely per token, according to reporting on Monday 2026-08-31.
